claim: A widely-accepted assumption is that the sensory organ is the first station in a serial chain of processing circuits leading to an internal circuit in which a percept emerges.
source: A widely-accepted assumption is that the sensory organ is the first station in a serial chain of processing circuits leading to an internal circuit in which a percept emerges.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific consensus in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: Until the midst of the 20th century psychologists and psychophysicists viewed perception as a primarily active process.
source: Until the midst of the 20th century psychologists and psychophysicists viewed perception as a primarily active process: perception is what emerges when an organism equipped with a brain interacts with its environment (James, 1890; Koffka, 1935; Mach, 1959; Merleau-Ponty, 1962; Uexkull, 1926).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to historical works in psychology and psychophysics.

claim: Behavioral studies revealed that although mammals can perceive events or objects while being passive, most of the time mammalian individuals seek for objects and perceive the world via active body and sensor movements.
source: Indeed, behavioral studies revealed that although mammals can perceive events or objects while being passive, most of the time mammalian individuals seek for objects and perceive the world via active body and sensor movements (Ahissar and Arieli, 2001; Diamond et al., 2008; Findlay and Gilchrist, 2003; Halpern, 1983; Kleinfeld et al., 2006; Konig and Luksch, 1998; Land, 2006; Lederman and Klatzky, 1987; Najemnik and Geisler, 2005; Rucci et al., 2007; Schroeder et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Passive paradigms cannot reveal how sensory information is actually processed during active perception.
source: Crucially, however, passive paradigms cannot reveal how sensory information is actually processed during active perception (Ahissar and Arieli, 2001; Ennis et al., 2014; Maravall and Diamond, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies discussing the limitations of passive paradigms.

claim: The elimination of motor components from the experimental scheme yielded a parallel elimination of motor variables from the corresponding theoretical schemes, leaving models of perception as sensory-only open-loop schemes.
source: The elimination of motor components from the experimental scheme yielded a parallel elimination of motor variables from the corresponding theoretical schemes, leaving models of perception as sensory-only open-loop schemes (e.g., Connor and Johnson, 1992; Edelman, 1993; Marr, 1982; Poggio and Serre, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical models of perception.

claim: An appropriate reductionist paradigm should leave the motor-object-sensory interactions intact.
source: This is not to say that any reduction would fail, but to emphasize that an appropriate reductionist paradigm should leave the motor-object-sensory interactions intact.
evidence: This is a theoretical assertion about what constitutes an appropriate experimental paradigm, based on inference from the limitations of current approaches.

claim: The OLP doctrine holds that external objects and features are perceived in an open-loop manner, in the motor-sensory sense.
source: The OLP doctrine holds that external objects and features are perceived in an open-loop manner, in the motor-sensory sense (Baars, 2002; Dehaene et al., 1998; Hochstein and Ahissar, 2002; Riesenhuber and Poggio, 2000; Tononi and Koch, 2008; Ullman, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to works representing the OLP doctrine.

claim: None of the characterized neuronal representations was shown so far to be the invariant representation of a specific external object or feature.
source: Crucially, however, although partial invariance had been demonstrated for portions of the proposed NRs in some of the cases, none of these NRs was shown so far to be "the" IvR of a specific external object or feature, namely an NR that is (at least substantially) invariant to changes in the most relevant conditions of perception.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the review of existing literature on neuronal representations.

claim: Across a large set of stimuli it was found that, depending on practice, exposure times as short as a few tens of milliseconds already allow a categorization of the presented stimulus, at least in a binary manner.
source: Across a large set of stimuli it was found that, depending on practice, exposure times as short as a few tens of milliseconds already allow a categorization of the presented stimulus, at least in a binary manner.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from psychophysical experiments.

claim: Mammalian sensory organs usually acquire information via movements.
source: Mammalian sensory organs usually acquire information via movements (Ahissar and Arieli, 2001; Chapin and Woodward, 1982; Diamond et al., 2008; Kleinfeld et al., 2006; Konig and Luksch, 1998; Land, 2006; Lederman and Klatzky, 1987; Prescott et al., 2011; Rucci et al., 2007; Schroeder et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on sensory organ movements.

claim: Visual and tactile systems employ movements of sensory organs that contain two-dimensional arrays of receptors.
source: Visual and tactile systems, for example, employ movements of sensory organs that contain two-dimensional arrays of receptors.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical and physiological knowledge.

claim: Larger movements (e.g., ocular saccades and head or arm movements) quickly move the array of receptors from one region of interest to another.
source: Larger movements (e.g., ocular saccades and head or arm movements) quickly move the array of receptors from one region of interest to another.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about sensory motor behavior.

claim: Smaller (and slower) movements (e.g., fixational drifts and finger or vibrissal scanning) scan the region of interest at fine resolution.
source: Smaller (and slower) movements (e.g., fixational drifts and finger or vibrissal scanning) scan the region of interest at fine resolution (Ahissar and Arieli, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on sensory scanning movements.

claim: The move-dwell-move pattern is typical for perceptual exploration across a large range of temporal scales, from minutes to less than a second.
source: This move-dwell-move pattern is typical for perceptual exploration across a large range of temporal scales, from minutes to less than a second (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2, which shows examples of this pattern.

claim: During sensor scanning, activations of individual receptors are functions of the interactions between the moving sensor and the physical features of external objects.
source: During sensor scanning, activations of individual (e.g., photo- or mechano-) receptors are functions of the interactions between the moving sensor and the physical features of external objects (Ahissar and Arieli, 2012; Ahissar and Vaadia, 1990; Bagdasarian et al., 2013; Boubenec et al., 2012; Friston, 2010; Gamzu and Ahissar, 2001; Gibson, 1962; Hires et al., 2013; Horev et al., 2011; Jarvilehto, 1999; Kuang et al., 2012; Mainland and Sobel, 2006; O'Regan and Noe, 2001; Pammer et al., 2013; Quist and Hartmann, 2012; Quist et al., 2014; Rucci and Victor, 2015; Saig et al., 2012; Saraf-Sinik et al., 2015; Smear et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by numerous citations to studies on motor-sensory interactions.

claim: The fact that mammalian sensation is active significantly challenges the OLP doctrine.
source: The fact that mammalian sensation is active significantly challenges the OLP doctrine.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that sensation is active and the implications for OLP.

claim: In vibrissal touch, a crucial sensory variable is the whisker curvature, which cannot be physically mimicked with only external forces.
source: In vibrissal touch, for example, a crucial sensory variable is the whisker curvature (Bagdasarian et al., 2013; Boubenec et al., 2012; Quist and Hartmann, 2012), which cannot be physically mimicked with only external forces (Bagdasarian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on whisker curvature and its role in touch.

claim: Ocular saccades are accompanied by peri-saccadic suppression during which activity along the visual sensory pathway is significantly suppressed.
source: Ocular saccades are accompanied by peri-saccadic suppression during which, unlike with flashed stimuli, activity along the visual sensory pathway is significantly suppressed (Hamker et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on peri-saccadic suppression.

claim: When compared, the characteristics of neuronal representations revealed with passive sensors are substantially different from those revealed with active sensors.
source: It is thus not surprising that, when compared, the characteristics of NRs revealed with passive sensors are substantially different from those revealed with active sensors (e.g., Kagan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study comparing passive and active sensing.

claim: When the assumption that presentation of an object retrieves its neuronal invariant representation was tested computationally at the presence of simulated eye movements, it was found that such a retrieval is possible with a very simple environment (one stimulus) and a limited number of possible neuronal representations (two).
source: When this assumption was tested computationally at the presence of simulated eye movements it was found that such a retrieval is possible with a very simple environment (one stimulus) and a limited number of possible NRs (two), in which case the knowledge of the statistics of sensor motion (e.g., eye movements) can provide unique, unambiguous solutions (Pitkow et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a computational study.

claim: The temporal code appears to be much more accurate, and of higher spatial resolution, than the spatial code in vision.
source: In fact, the temporal code appears to be much more accurate, and of higher spatial resolution, than the spatial code (Ahissar and Arieli, 2012; Berry et al., 1997; Reich et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies comparing temporal and spatial coding.

claim: Sensory signals may often be ambiguous if processed without the motor signals that yielded them.
source: Sensory signals may often be ambiguous if processed without the motor signals that yielded them.
evidence: This is a general assertion supported by specific examples provided in the text.

claim: The same whisker curvature can be generated when contacting objects at different locations, an ambiguity that is resolved if the angle by which the whisker is rotated is taken into account.
source: One example is the curvature signal generated at the base of a whisker upon its contact with an object. The same curvature can be generated when contacting objects at different locations, an ambiguity that is resolved if the angle by which the whisker is rotated is taken into account (Bagdasarian et al., 2013) (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 3, which illustrates the concept.

claim: In vivo recordings from the primate retina ruled out pure sensory processing, such as lateral inhibition, as a basis for edge detection while supporting motor-sensory processes involving eye movements.
source: Consistently, in vivo recordings from the primate retina ruled out pure sensory processing, such as lateral inhibition, as a basis for edge detection while supporting motor-sensory processes involving eye movements (Ennis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an in vivo recording study.

claim: Retinal information depends on the nature and trajectory of miniature eye movements.
source: For vision this is further supported by a series of experiments and analyses indicating that retinal information depends on the nature and trajectory of miniature eye movements (Ahissar et al., 2014; Ko et al., 2010; Kuang et al., 2012; Olveczky et al., 2003; Rucci et al., 2007; Snodderly et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on eye movements and retinal information.

claim: Efference copies are not accurate enough to account for perceptual accuracy.
source: Note that this challenge cannot be alleviated by adding efference copy information to open-loop perceptual processing – efference copies are not accurate enough to account for perceptual accuracy (Ahissar et al., 2015a; Pitkow et al., 2007; Simony et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on efference copy accuracy.

claim: Perception of object location in rats depends on the details of the motor trajectory at a resolution corresponding to movements induced by individual motor spikes.
source: For example, perception of object location in rats (Knutsen and Ahissar, 2009) depends on the details of the motor trajectory at a resolution corresponding to movements induced by individual motor spikes (Herfst and Brecht, 2008; Simony et al., 2008), a resolution that is likely not available in internal efference copies (Fee et al., 1997; Hill et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on motor trajectory and perception in rats.

claim: The accuracy of visual efference copies is two orders of magnitude lower than the size of fine eye movements.
source: Similarly, the accuracy of visual efference copies is two orders of magnitude lower than the size of fine eye movements (Pitkow et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on visual efference copy accuracy.

claim: Sensory organs are associated with muscles whose activations move the sensory organ and induce sensory signals.
source: Sensory organs (eyes, hands, whiskers) are associated with muscles whose activations move the sensory organ and induce sensory signals (Simony et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on established anatomical and physiological knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: The neuronal motor and sensory systems that are associated with a given sensory organ are connected via an intricate system of loops that does not allow an isolated operation of either.
source: The neuronal motor and sensory systems that are associated with a given sensory organ are connected via an intricate system of loops that does not allow an isolated operation of either (see illustration of the vibrissal system in Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 4A, which illustrates the loop connections.

claim: When motor efferents of a specific sensory organ are activated, sensory signals are inevitably generated.
source: When motor efferents of a specific sensory organ are activated, sensory signals are inevitably generated (Hentschke et al., 2006; Jarvilehto, 1999; Johansson and Flanagan, 2009; Keller et al., 2012; Poulet and Petersen, 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on motor-sensory coupling.

claim: When sensory signals are generated, motor efferents to the same sensory organ are naturally affected.
source: and when sensory signals are generated, motor efferents to the same sensory organ are naturally affected (Bonneh et al., 2013; Gilad et al., 2014; Ko et al., 2010; Mainland and Sobel, 2006; Nguyen and Kleinfeld, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on sensory-motor feedback.

claim: Visual MSM-loops follow a multi-pathway architecture with sensory information feeding back onto oculomotor pathways at virtually all brain levels.
source: Existing anatomical descriptions of Visual MSM-loops are less detailed, although it is known that they also follow a multi-pathway architecture (Bishop, 1959; Casagrande, 1994; Diamond, 1983; Lappe et al., 1999; Nassi and Callaway, 2009; Wang et al., 2007), with sensory information feeding back onto oculomotor pathways at virtually all brain levels (Dhande and Huberman, 2014; Fries et al., 1985; Guillery, 2005; Guillery and Sherman, 2002; Krauzlis and Lisberger, 1991; Malik et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The closed-loop architecture of the perceptual systems challenges the OLP doctrine.
source: The closed-loop architecture of the perceptual systems challenges the OLP doctrine.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical evidence of closed-loop connections.

claim: Increased stimulus exposure durations increase perceptual accuracy and confidence.
source: Moreover, it is known that increased stimulus exposure durations increase perceptual accuracy and confidence (Packer and Williams, 1992; Saig et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to psychophysical studies.

claim: The presentation of a second object within tens of milliseconds after the presentation of a target object prevents or impairs the perception of this target object.
source: The presentation of a second object within tens of milliseconds after the presentation of a target object prevents or impairs the perception of this target object (Enns and Di Lollo, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on backward masking.

claim: Experimental data on backward masking were found to be inconsistent with open loop schemes, while supporting a dependency of perception on closed loop mechanisms, in which the stimulus is repetitively sampled.
source: Experimental data, however, were found to be inconsistent with such open loop schemes, while supporting a dependency of perception on closed loop ("re-entrant") mechanisms, in which the stimulus is repetitively sampled (Enns and Di Lollo, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on backward masking mechanisms.

claim: Typical perceptual epochs last hundreds of milliseconds.
source: Perception takes time – typical perceptual epochs last hundreds of milliseconds.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from perceptual studies.

claim: The first wave of sensory-driven neuronal activity typically reaches most of the relevant cortical areas within ~100 milliseconds.
source: The first wave of sensory-driven neuronal activity typically reaches most of the relevant cortical areas within ~100 milliseconds
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from neurophysiological studies.

claim: Quick saccadic reports on the crude category of the perceived item can be generated as fast as 150 milliseconds after stimulus onset.
source: and quick saccadic reports on the crude category of the perceived item can be generated as fast as 150 milliseconds after stimulus onset (Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on rapid categorization.

claim: The identification of more delicate categories and the perception of item details take typically hundreds of milliseconds from first sensor-object encounter, a period during which perceptual acuity continuously improves.
source: Yet, the identification of more delicate categories and the perception of item details take typically hundreds of milliseconds from first sensor-object encounter, a period during which perceptual acuity continuously improves (Micheyl et al., 2012; Packer and Williams, 1992; Saig et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on perceptual processing time.

claim: Perceptual thresholds are correlated with neuronal activities that are recorded after the first transient neuronal response.
source: Consistently, scalp EEG recordings reveal that perceptual thresholds are correlated with neuronal activities that are recorded after the first transient neuronal response (Censor et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an EEG study.

claim: Object features, such as location and texture, are perceived via a sequence of sensor-object interactions whose motor and sensory variables show a pattern of convergence towards asymptotic values.
source: Careful analyses of rodent and human behavior during tactile perception reveal signatures of a converging process. Object features, such as location and texture, are perceived via a sequence of sensor-object interactions whose motor and sensory variables show a pattern of convergence towards asymptotic values (Chen et al., 2015; Horev et al., 2011; Knutsen et al., 2006; McDermott et al., 2013; Saig et al., 2012; Saraf-Sinik et al., 2015; Voigts et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Converging dynamics are hallmarks of closed-loops – an open-loop system does not converge as a whole.
source: Converging dynamics, i.e., dynamics during which the state of the entire system gradually approaches a steady state, are hallmarks of closed-loops – an open-loop system does not converge as a whole.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from dynamical systems theory.

claim: Perception of external objects is a closed-loop dynamical process encompassing loops that integrate the organism and its environment and converging towards organism-environment steady-states.
source: We present here a hypothesis in which the perception of external objects is a closed-loop dynamical process encompassing loops that integrate the organism and its environment and converging towards organism-environment steady-states.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the paper, presented as a theoretical proposition.

claim: Perception is a process in which the brain temporarily 'grasps' external objects and incorporates them in its MSM-loops.
source: CLP suggests that perception of the external environment is a process in which the brain temporarily 'grasps' external objects and incorporates them in its MSM-loops.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposition that is part of the CLP hypothesis.

claim: A given percept is associated with a given steady-state of the motor-sensory-neuronal variables space.
source: Our hypothesis thus asserts that a given percept is associated with a given steady-state of the motor-sensory-neuronal variables space.
evidence: This is a theoretical assertion that is part of the CLP hypothesis.

claim: The SYCLOP platform demonstrates a simple CLP convergence process and shows how different percepts can be differentiated in CLP.
source: This implementation illustrates a simple CLP convergence process (Figure 5) and shows how different precepts can be differentiated in CLP.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the SYCLOP implementation and reference to Figure 5.

claim: In the SYCLOP implementation, a monotonic change in contrast results in a corresponding monotonic change of the limit cycle.
source: Importantly, in all these phase planes the limit cycle depends on the external contrast (γ); while maintaining all loop parameters constant, a monotonic change in γ results in a corresponding monotonic change of the limit cycle (green and red trajectories in Figure 6E for contrasts of 0.5 and 0.9, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CLP predicts that, although the percepts evoked by flashed stimuli can be robust, they would typically include significantly less information than the information actively acquired from continuously-present objects during typical perceptual epochs.
source: CLP thus predicts that, although the percepts evoked by flashed stimuli can be robust, they would typically include significantly less information than the information actively acquired from continuously-present objects during typical perceptual epochs.
evidence: This is a testable prediction derived from the CLP hypothesis.

claim: Artificially flashed stimuli initiate a perceptual process, and provide some perceptual information, but do not allow further accumulation of perceptual information as would normally occur with natural stationary objects.
source: According to CLP, thus, artificially flashed stimuli initiate a perceptual process, and provide some perceptual information, but do not allow further accumulation of perceptual information as would normally occur with natural stationary objects (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a theoretical assertion derived from the CLP hypothesis, illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: A congenital ophthalmoplegic patient who had no eye movements since birth developed a pattern of head movements that resembled that of natural eye movements.
source: Regarding vision, we are aware of only one study analysing visual perception in a congenital ophthalmoplegic patient, a patient who had no eye movements since birth; in this case, the patient developed a pattern of head movements that resembled that of natural eye movements, only on a slower rhythm (Gilchrist et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a case study.

claim: Natural employment of active vision is indicated by the 'weird, confusing and indescribable' forms of perceptions reported during acute partial paralysis of the ocular muscles.
source: Natural employment of active vision is indicated by the "weird, confusing and indescribable" forms of perceptions reported during acute partial paralysis of the ocular muscles (Stevens et al., 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on ocular muscle paralysis.

claim: CLP proposes a reconciliation of objective scientific observations and subjective everyday experience via closed-loop dynamics between the perceiver and the perceived.
source: Our CLP hypothesis proposes a reconciliation of objective scientific observations and subjective everyday experience via closed-loop dynamics between the perceiver and the perceived.
evidence: This is a philosophical implication of the CLP hypothesis.
